title: Nitrofurantoin and Alcohol: Can You Drink on Macrobid?
excerpt: Can you drink on nitrofurantoin (Macrobid, mono-mcr)? What the interaction really is, why alcohol can make a UTI feel worse, how long to wait, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on nitrofurantoin (Macrobid)? The real interaction, why alcohol can worsen a UTI, how long to wait after your last dose, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no well-documented dangerous chemical reaction between nitrofurantoin (Macrobid, Macrodantin) and alcohol. It is not like metronidazole, where drinking can cause a violent flushing and vomiting reaction. Nitrofurantoin's official US prescribing information does not list alcohol as something you must avoid. That said, "no dangerous reaction" is not the same as "a good idea." Alcohol and nitrofurantoin share several side effects, most notably nausea, dizziness, and headache, so drinking can make the antibiotic harder to tolerate. Alcohol also irritates the bladder and makes you urinate more, which is the last thing an already-inflamed bladder needs. For most people with a simple bladder infection, the smartest choice is to skip alcohol for the few days you're on the medicine.

**The quick rules:** A single drink while on nitrofurantoin is unlikely to be dangerous for a healthy adult, but it may make you feel worse and can aggravate UTI symptoms. Avoid heavy drinking during the course. Take every dose with food, finish the full course even if you feel better, and drink plenty of water. If you develop fever, chills, back or side pain, vomiting, trouble breathing, or a cough that comes on suddenly, contact a doctor promptly, whether or not you've been drinking.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your medicine and knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on nitrofurantoin if** you have kidney problems, liver disease, diabetes, nerve problems, lung disease, or G6PD deficiency, if you're pregnant or breastfeeding, if you take nitrofurantoin long term to prevent infections, or if you drink heavily on a regular basis. **Get medical care promptly if** you have fever, chills, pain in your back or side, vomiting, blood in your urine that doesn't clear, no improvement after two or three days, sudden shortness of breath or chest pain, or yellow skin or eyes. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Nitrofurantoin and Alcohol Actually Interact

To understand why this combination is mostly about comfort rather than danger, it helps to know how nitrofurantoin works.

Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic used almost entirely for **bladder infections** (cystitis), the most common kind of urinary tract infection. It's unusual among antibiotics. After you swallow it, very little of it stays in your blood. Instead, your kidneys filter it rapidly into your urine, where it reaches high concentrations right where the bacteria are living. Inside bacterial cells, the drug is converted into reactive compounds that damage the bacteria's DNA, proteins, and other machinery. Because it attacks bacteria in several ways at once, resistance to nitrofurantoin has stayed relatively low compared with some other UTI antibiotics.

That design explains both its strengths and its limits:

- **It works well in the bladder**, because that's where it concentrates.
- **It does not work well for kidney infections** or infections in the bloodstream, because levels in body tissues stay low.
- **It depends on healthy kidneys**, because the kidneys have to concentrate it into the urine.

Alcohol, by contrast, is mostly processed by your liver. The two substances largely travel different routes through the body. There is no strong evidence that a moderate amount of alcohol meaningfully changes how much nitrofurantoin reaches your urine or how well it kills bacteria.

### Does nitrofurantoin cause a "disulfiram-like" reaction?

You may have seen warnings online claiming that nitrofurantoin causes the same severe reaction as metronidazole or the alcoholism drug disulfiram (Antabuse): sudden flushing, pounding heart, nausea, and vomiting after a drink. Nitrofurantoin belongs to a family of drugs called nitrofurans, and a few older nitrofuran compounds were associated with reactions like this. That's likely where the warning comes from.

For nitrofurantoin itself, though, this reaction is not well established. It isn't listed as a known interaction in the current US prescribing information, and it doesn't appear in the standard interaction warnings pharmacists use day to day. That doesn't mean no one has ever felt sick after drinking on it. It means there's no good evidence that it's a predictable chemical reaction the way it is with metronidazole. If you do feel flushed, nauseated, or unwell after a drink, stop drinking, and mention it to your pharmacist.

### Does alcohol make nitrofurantoin less effective?

There is no good evidence that a drink or two stops nitrofurantoin from working. The bigger risks to your treatment are behavioral, and they're real:

- **Missed or late doses.** A night out is a common reason people forget an evening dose or take it hours late. Nitrofurantoin needs steady levels in your urine to keep the bacteria down.
- **Taking it on an empty stomach.** The label says to take nitrofurantoin with food. Food improves how much of the drug you absorb and makes nausea less likely. Late-night drinking and skipped meals work against that.
- **Vomiting.** If alcohol or the medicine makes you throw up soon after a dose, some of that dose may be lost.
- **Stopping early.** Feeling better after two days and celebrating with a drink is common. Stopping the antibiotic at that point raises the chance the infection comes back.

So the honest framing is this: alcohol is unlikely to neutralize the drug directly, but it makes it easier to take the drug badly.

## Shared Side Effects: Why You May Feel Worse

This is the main practical reason to skip alcohol during a course. Nitrofurantoin's most common side effects overlap with how alcohol and hangovers make you feel.

| Side effect | From nitrofurantoin | From alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Nausea | One of the most common side effects | Common, especially the next day |
| Headache | Common | Classic hangover symptom |
| Dizziness or drowsiness | Listed side effect | Well known effect |
| Upset stomach, loss of appetite | Common | Common, alcohol irritates the stomach lining |
| Diarrhea | Can occur, as with most antibiotics | Common after heavy drinking |

When you stack two things that each cause nausea and dizziness, you tend to feel more of both. The nausea is especially worth taking seriously. If you feel sick enough to skip food or skip doses, your treatment suffers.

There's also a timing issue. A rough morning after drinking can hide early warning signs that something is going wrong, such as a fever, unusual tiredness, or feeling generally unwell. People sometimes write those off as a hangover. If you're on any antibiotic and feel worse instead of better, don't assume it's just the alcohol.

## Alcohol and a UTI: The Bladder Problem

Even setting the antibiotic aside, alcohol is not a friend to an infected bladder.

- **Alcohol is a diuretic.** It reduces a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you urinate more. With a UTI, that means more trips to the bathroom and more of the burning and urgency you're already dealing with.- **It can irritate the bladder lining.** Alcohol, along with caffeine, carbonated drinks, and acidic mixers, is commonly listed as a bladder irritant. Many people with UTIs or bladder sensitivity notice that drinking makes urgency and discomfort worse.
- **It dehydrates you.** You lose more fluid than you take in, and dehydration can make urine more concentrated and stinging. Drinking plenty of water is one of the standard pieces of UTI self-care, and alcohol pushes in the opposite direction.
- **It can affect your immune response.** Heavy drinking, including a single binge, is known to dampen parts of the immune system for a while. A moderate drink isn't going to stop your recovery, but a big night out while you're fighting an infection isn't helping either. Our article on [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) covers this in more depth.

If you feel you really want a drink, waiting until the course is finished and your symptoms have cleared is the easier path for most people. A typical course for an uncomplicated bladder infection is short, so it's usually only a few days.

## Macrobid, Macrodantin, and "Mono-Mcr": Are They Different With Alcohol?

You might see nitrofurantoin under several names on your prescription bottle. They're the same active drug in different forms, and the alcohol advice is the same for all of them.

- **Macrobid** is a brand of **nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals**. Pharmacy labels often shorten this to "nitrofurantoin mono-mcr" or "nitrofurantoin monohyd/m-cryst." It's usually taken **twice a day**, about 12 hours apart, with food.
- **Macrodantin** is a brand of **nitrofurantoin macrocrystals**. It's usually taken **four times a day** with food.
- **Furadantin** is a liquid suspension, used mostly for children.

The "macrocrystal" forms are designed to release the drug more slowly, which tends to cause less nausea than older forms. But they don't change anything about alcohol. If your bottle says "mono-mcr," everything in this article applies to you.

The twice-a-day schedule matters for drinking. If you take your evening dose of Macrobid with dinner and then go out, you're drinking on top of a fresh dose. If you postpone the dose until you get home, it may be late, on an empty stomach, and possibly forgotten. Neither is ideal. If you do decide to have a drink, take the dose on time with a proper meal first.

### What if I'm on nitrofurantoin long term?

Some people take a low daily dose of nitrofurantoin for months to prevent repeat UTIs. Long-term use carries different risks than a five-day course. The rare but serious side effects described below, especially lung reactions, liver inflammation, and nerve damage, are more often linked to long-term use. Heavy drinking also strains the liver and can damage nerves on its own. If you take nitrofurantoin long term, talk to your doctor about how much alcohol, if any, is reasonable for you, and keep up with any blood tests they recommend.

## Can I Have One Drink on Nitrofurantoin?

For a healthy adult on a short course, one drink is unlikely to cause a dangerous reaction. Here's how to think about it realistically:

1. **There's no strong evidence of a dangerous interaction.** That's the reassuring part.
2. **You may still feel worse.** More nausea, more headache, more dizziness, and possibly more bladder discomfort.
3. **Your infection may be slower to settle.** Not because alcohol disables the drug, but because of dehydration, bladder irritation, and the habits that come with drinking.
4. **The course is short.** For a typical bladder infection, you're usually looking at a handful of days. Waiting until it's over costs very little.

If you do have a drink, keep it to one, have it with food, drink water alongside it, and don't let it shift your dose schedule. Avoid anything that looks like a big night: several drinks, shots, or drinking on an empty stomach. And if you're the kind of person who often wakes up needing something for a headache after drinking, be careful about what you reach for. Painkillers have their own alcohol issues, which we cover in our guides to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).

## How Long After Nitrofurantoin Can I Drink?

Nitrofurantoin leaves the body quickly. Its half-life in the blood is short, well under an hour in people with normal kidney function, and most of it is cleared within a day of the last dose. So from a drug-clearance point of view, there's no long waiting period like the one recommended after metronidazole.

A more useful rule is to wait until **two things are true**:

- **You've finished the full course.** Every dose, even if you felt better after day two.
- **Your symptoms are gone.** If you still have burning, urgency, or discomfort, your bladder is still inflamed, and alcohol may aggravate it.

For most people, that means waiting until the day after your last dose and checking that you feel back to normal. If your symptoms haven't cleared by the end of the course, don't drink to "see how it goes." Call your doctor, because the infection may need a different antibiotic.

## Rare but Serious Side Effects to Know About

Nitrofurantoin is widely used and generally safe for short courses. But it has a few uncommon side effects that you should recognize, because some can look like other things, including a hangover or a cold. None of these are caused by alcohol, but they're important to know whether you drink or not.

- **Lung reactions.** Rarely, nitrofurantoin can cause a sudden allergic-type lung reaction, sometimes within hours to days of starting it. Signs include fever, chills, cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath. A slower form can develop with long-term use, showing up as a gradual cough and breathlessness. Either one needs prompt medical attention.
- **Liver inflammation.** Hepatitis is a rare side effect, more often seen with long-term use. Signs include yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, pain under the right ribs, and unusual tiredness. Heavy drinking is hard on the liver too, which is one more reason to keep alcohol low if you're on this medicine for months.
- **Nerve damage (peripheral neuropathy).** Nitrofurantoin can rarely cause numbness, tingling, or burning in the hands and feet. The prescribing information lists kidney problems, diabetes, anemia, electrolyte imbalances, and vitamin B deficiency as factors that raise the risk. Heavy, long-term drinking can cause its own nerve damage and B-vitamin deficiencies. Report any tingling or numbness to your doctor right away.
- **Hemolytic anemia.** People with an inherited condition called G6PD deficiency can have red blood cells break down on nitrofurantoin. Signs include unusual tiredness, pale or yellow skin, and dark urine.
- **Severe diarrhea.** As with almost any antibiotic, nitrofurantoin can rarely lead to a bowel infection called *C. difficile*, which causes watery diarrhea that doesn't stop, sometimes with cramps or fever. This can happen during treatment or weeks afterward.

**One harmless side effect:** nitrofurantoin often turns urine dark yellow or brown. That's expected and isn't a sign of liver trouble on its own. But if dark urine comes with yellow eyes or skin, or pale stools, call your doctor.

## Other Things That Matter More Than Alcohol

If you're trying to get the most out of nitrofurantoin, these factors have a clearer effect than a single drink.

- **Take it with food.** This is on the label for a reason. It improves absorption and reduces nausea.
- **Avoid antacids containing magnesium trisilicate.** The prescribing information notes that these can reduce how much nitrofurantoin you absorb. If you use antacids for heartburn after drinking, ask a pharmacist which ones are fine to take, and space them apart from your dose.
- **Tell your doctor about your kidneys.** Nitrofurantoin isn't recommended when kidney function is significantly reduced, because the drug can't reach effective levels in the urine and side effect risk goes up.
- **Know when it's the wrong drug.** If you have a fever, back or side pain, or vomiting, the infection may have spread to your kidneys. Nitrofurantoin isn't designed for kidney infections, so this needs a doctor's review, not just more of the same pills.
- **Pregnancy.** Nitrofurantoin is often used for UTIs during pregnancy, but it's generally avoided near the end of pregnancy. Alcohol is best avoided entirely during pregnancy. Follow your prenatal care provider's advice.

## When to See a Doctor

Most uncomplicated bladder infections start improving within a day or two of starting nitrofurantoin. Contact your doctor or get care if:

- You have **fever, chills, or pain in your back or side**, which can mean a kidney infection
- You're **vomiting** and can't keep doses down
- Your symptoms **aren't improving after two to three days** or come back soon after you finish
- You see **blood in your urine** that doesn't clear
- You develop **sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or a new cough** while on the medicine
- You notice **yellow skin or eyes, numbness or tingling, or severe diarrhea**

**Go to the emergency room or call 911** if you have trouble breathing, signs of a severe allergic reaction (swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or a widespread rash), confusion, or a high fever with shaking chills.

And separate from the antibiotic: if you've been drinking heavily and notice confusion, repeated vomiting, very slow or irregular breathing, or someone can't be woken up, treat that as a possible alcohol poisoning emergency and call 911.

## Could a Hangover Supplement Help?

If your question is really "how do I drink without feeling awful," it's worth being straight with you: while you're treating a UTI, the best plan is not to drink at all. No supplement changes that. Once your course is finished and you're feeling well, the basics matter most: pace yourself, eat beforehand, alternate with water, and know your limits. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising but not proven, and there's no good evidence that it interacts with nitrofurantoin one way or the other, simply because it hasn't been studied together. That's a reason to wait until you've finished your antibiotic before trying it, and to check with your pharmacist if you're on long-term nitrofurantoin. If you do decide to try DHM later, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take, and our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about mixing supplements with prescription drugs.

## The Bottom Line

- There is **no well-established dangerous reaction** between nitrofurantoin and alcohol, and the US label doesn't list alcohol as a contraindication.
- The claim that nitrofurantoin causes a metronidazole-style flushing and vomiting reaction is **not well supported** for this drug.
- Alcohol and nitrofurantoin share side effects like **nausea, headache, and dizziness**, so drinking can make treatment harder to tolerate.
- Alcohol **irritates the bladder, increases urination, and dehydrates you**, which can make UTI symptoms worse and recovery slower.
- Macrobid, Macrodantin, and "mono-mcr" are all nitrofurantoin. **The advice is the same for all of them.**
- The simplest choice is to **skip alcohol until you've finished the course and your symptoms are gone.** If you have one drink, have it with food and water and keep your doses on schedule.
- Get care promptly for **fever, back pain, vomiting, breathing problems, or no improvement after two to three days.**

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking nitrofurantoin?**

There is no well-documented dangerous interaction between nitrofurantoin and alcohol, and the US prescribing information doesn't list alcohol as something you must avoid. Still, most doctors and pharmacists suggest skipping alcohol during the course. Alcohol shares side effects with the drug (nausea, headache, dizziness), irritates the bladder, and dehydrates you, all of which can make a UTI feel worse. If you have kidney, liver, or nerve problems, or you take nitrofurantoin long term, ask your doctor first.

**Does nitrofurantoin cause a reaction with alcohol like metronidazole does?**

Not in any well-established way. Metronidazole is known for a flushing, nausea, and vomiting reaction with alcohol. Some older drugs in nitrofurantoin's chemical family were linked to similar reactions, which is likely where the warning comes from, but there's no good evidence that nitrofurantoin itself causes this predictably. If you feel flushed or sick after drinking on it, stop drinking and tell your pharmacist.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking Macrobid?**

Macrobid is a brand of nitrofurantoin, so the same advice applies. There's no known dangerous reaction, but alcohol can worsen nausea, headache, and bladder irritation. Because Macrobid is usually taken twice a day with food, drinking also makes it easier to take an evening dose late, on an empty stomach, or not at all. The simplest approach is to wait until you've finished the course.

**What is nitrofurantoin mono-mcr, and is it safe with alcohol?**

"Nitrofurantoin mono-mcr" is a pharmacy abbreviation for nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals, the same form as the brand Macrobid. It's the same active drug, so the alcohol advice is identical: no well-established dangerous interaction, but drinking can make side effects and UTI symptoms worse. Take each dose with food and finish the full course.

**How long after taking nitrofurantoin can I drink alcohol?**

Nitrofurantoin is cleared from the body quickly, so there's no long waiting period like there is with metronidazole. A sensible rule is to wait until you've taken your last dose and your UTI symptoms have fully cleared, which for most people means the day after finishing the course. If you still have symptoms when the course ends, contact your doctor rather than drinking.

**Will alcohol make my UTI worse?**

It can. Alcohol makes you urinate more, can irritate the bladder lining, and dehydrates you, which may increase burning and urgency. Heavy drinking can also temporarily weaken parts of your immune response. One drink won't usually derail treatment, but avoiding alcohol and drinking plenty of water is the better way to help your bladder recover.

**Does alcohol stop nitrofurantoin from working?**

There's no good evidence that moderate drinking directly makes nitrofurantoin less effective. The bigger risk is indirect: missed or late doses, taking the medicine without food, vomiting a dose, or stopping the course early. Any of those can make treatment less likely to work. Keep your doses on time and with food.

**Is it safe to take a painkiller for a hangover while on nitrofurantoin?**

There's no known major interaction between nitrofurantoin and common over-the-counter painkillers, but those painkillers have their own alcohol risks. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) can stress the liver after heavy drinking, and ibuprofen can irritate the stomach and strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated. Ask a pharmacist if you're unsure, take the lowest label dose with food and water, and avoid antacids containing magnesium trisilicate, which can reduce nitrofurantoin absorption.
